To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

mitochondrial membrane potential and the permeability transition are relatively stable through 2 years of age in both cortical and striatal regions, but that cortical mitochondria become more susceptible to the calcium‐induced permeability transition at advanced ages.

mitochondrial function is stable through the majority of the lifespan in both brain regions and that mitochondrial function declines in the cortex, but not in the striatum, only at very advanced ages.

the permeability transition is more sensitive to calcium at advanced ages in the cerebral cortex than in the striatum, and that mitochondrial function declines with age, but the decline is relatively small.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the mechanisms of age‐related changes in mitochondrial function.
the effects of aging on brain mitochondria.
the effects of aging upon mitochondrial function in the brain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
mitochondrial function in the striatum declines with aging, whereas in the cortex it does not.
mitochondrial function is not dramatically altered in the brain with aging, but rather that there is a slight decline in function with advanced age.

mitochondria from both striatum and cortex of Fischer 344 rats are relatively stable through the second year of life, and that the mitochondria from the striatum are more sensitive to calcium and more resistant to calcium‐induced swelling than are the cortical mitochondria.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the ability of mitochondria from both cortical and striatal regions to maintain polarization and resist calcium‐mediated swelling and depolarizations remains remarkably stable throughout most of the life span of Fischer 344 rats.
mitochondrial function is remarkably stable with aging, although subtle changes in function are detectable in both brain regions.
the ability to maintain mitochondrial membrane potential is preserved in both striatal and cortical mitochondria through 24 months.
The main takeaway from our work is that
mitochondrial function is remarkably stable throughout the first 24 months of life and that the permeability transition is not a major factor in the aging brain.
the brain mitochondria from rats remain remarkably stable in their ability to respond to calcium through 24 months.
mitochondria in the aging rat brain are remarkably resistant to age‐related changes in their function.
